Plot1.funFact: Veld grape and dragon fruit  look very similar, often causing confusion among gardeners.

Open area 2A.uses: Sericulture (Silk Production): White mulberry leaves serve as the primary, indispensable food source for silkworms.Culinary Arts: The sweet, tart fruits are eaten fresh or processed into jams, juices, wines, pies, and tarts.Traditional Medicine: Practitioners of Traditional Chinese Medicine use the root bark, leaves, and fruit to address coughs, fever, and blood sugar regulation.
Open area 2A.funFact: Not a True Berry: Botanically speaking, a mulberry is not a berry at all but a "multiple fruit" formed from a cluster of independent flowers.Super-Sonic Pollen: The flowers of the white mulberry tree can fire pollen at over half the speed of sound, making it one of the fastest movements in the plant kingdom.

Open area 2B.uses: Medicinal Infusions: In the Philippines, the leaves are widely boiled to create a medicinal tea used to treat coughs, diarrhea, colic, and dysentery
Open area 2B.funFact: Namesake Origins: It gets its name from the Fujian Province in southeastern China (often spelled Fukien in the past), where it has been grown for centuries and is mentioned in literature dating back to the Tang Dynasty.

Open area 2C.uses: Edible Greens: Highly nutritious and packed with protein and vitamins. The tender leaves are frequently boiled, stir-fried, or used as a nutrient-dense spinach substitute in soups, quiches, and omelettes. The flowers can be eaten raw in salads.
Open area 2C.funFact: Explosive Seed Pods: The plant produces seed pods that, when ripe and dry, split in half explosively to fling their seeds out into the surrounding area.It’s Not Actually Chinese: Despite its common name, the Chinese Violet is native to sub-Saharan Africa and India

Open area 2D.uses: Folk Medicine: Traditionally crushed, boiled, or dried to create herbal teas and poultices. It is empirically used to lower blood pressure, reduce cholesterol, manage diabetes, and heal wounds
Open area 2D.funFact: It’s Not Actually an Onion: Despite resembling shallots with its red skin and white rings, the Dayak onion belongs to the iris family (the same family as saffron) rather than the allium family.Evening Bloomers: The plant produces small, delicate five-petaled white or yellow flowers that bloom in the late afternoon and stay open for only a few hours.

Open area 2E.uses: Fresh Consumption: Eaten fresh out of hand when absolutely ripe (deep red or near-black) to avoid its bitter, resinous under-ripe tang.
Open area 2E.funFact: Folk Remedies: Teas made from the leaves are used as a folk treatment for stomachaches, colic, bronchitis, and heartburn.Blood Pressure: Traditional extracts have been studied for their natural antihypertensive properties.

Open area 2F.uses: The tree is primarily valued for its bright red-orange seeds, which provide a versatile natural pigment called annatto.Natural Food Coloring: It is one of the world's most common natural dyes, used to give cheese (like Cheddar), butter, margarine, ice cream, and rice their yellow or orange hues.
Open area 2F.funFact: The Name Origin: The "lipstick tree" nickname comes from indigenous people in Central and South America using the seed pulp as a natural cosmetic and body paint for ceremonies.Ancient Sunscreen: The Mayans and Aztecs used the pigment not just for color, but as a natural sunscreen and insect repellent.

Open area 2G.uses: Used in drinks, marinades, and desserts
Open area 2G.funFact: Prevented scurvy in sailors; highly acidic fruit.

Open area 2H.uses: Traditional Medicine: In Southeast Asia (especially Malaysia and Singapore), the raw or boiled leaves are used in folk medicine to treat cancer, rheumatism, gastric pain, and ulcers.Edible Fruits & Leaves: The fleshy, top-shaped yellow fruits are edible (though quite sour) and can be used in chili pastes or cocktails. The leaves can also be eaten raw in small quantities or used to make tea
Open area 2H.funFact: A Cactus with Leaves: Unlike nearly all other cacti, the Rose Cactus does not drop its leaves; it retains large, glossy green leaves year-round.Ancient Ancestry: Because it retains true leaves, it is considered a "primitive" or non-succulent cactus. It is basically an evolutionary stepping stone between normal leafy shrubs and desert cacti!

Open area 2I.uses: 1 Turmeric,  2 Black Turmeric,  3 Shell Ginger,   4 Shampoo Ginger,   5 Mango Ginger,   6 Torch Ginger,   7 Blue Ginger
Open area 2I.funFact: 1 Turmeric: Standard culinary spice used for vibrant yellow coloring in curries, anti-inflammatory supplements, and natural textiles dyes.  2 Black Turmeric: Rare medicinal root applied as a topical paste for sprains, snakebites, and cosmetic face masks.  3 Shell Ginger: Ornamental plant utilized for wrapping foods, brewing traditional herbal teas, and antioxidant skin care.  4 Shampoo Ginger: Sap from the flower cones serves as a natural, fragrant hair cleanser and scalp moisturizer.  5 Mango Ginger: Distinct raw-mango flavored rhizome ideal for fresh pickles, chutneys, and soothing digestive issues.   6 Torch Ginger: Edible pink flower buds highly prized as an aromatic ingredient in Southeast Asian salads, laksa, and curries.  7 Blue Ginger: Native Galangal variety primarily used to add a sharp, citrusy-earthy bite to Thai pastes and Indonesian dishes.
Open area 2I.botanical: Turmeric: Curcuma longa,  Black Turmeric: Curcuma caesia,  Shell Ginger: Alpinia zerumbet,  Shampoo Ginger: Zingiber zerumbet,  Mango Ginger: Curcuma amada,  Torch Ginger: Etlingera elatior,  Blue Ginger: Alpinia galanga

Open area 2J.uses: Culinary: The leaves are a staple leafy vegetable in many West and Central African cuisines (most famously in the Nigerian dish Ofe Onugbu). Because of their pungency, they are repeatedly squeezed and washed to remove excess bitterness before being added to stews.Traditional Medicine: The juice and leaf extracts are consumed as tonics or teas to alleviate malaria, control blood sugar in diabetics, and boost digestion.
Open area 2J.funFact: Domestic Applications: The strong, bitter woody stems are frequently broken down and used as natural "chewing sticks" to maintain dental hygiene and ward off mouth infections.

Open area 2K.uses: Skin Healing: It is widely known as the "ringworm bush". Crushed fresh leaves or sap contain chrysophanic acid, which naturally fights fungal infections like ringworm, athlete's foot, and eczema when applied topically.
Open area 2K.funFact: The candle bush gets its name because its unopened bright-yellow flower spikes resemble giant, glowing, waxy candles!

Open area 2L.uses: Culinary: Tubers are a rich source of complex carbohydrates and are eaten baked, boiled, mashed, or pounded into fufu. Purple varieties (Dioscorea alata) are prized for making desserts and ice cream.Nutritional: They provide high levels of dietary fiber, vitamin C, potassium, and B-complex vitamins.Medicinal: Yam tubers contain a compound called diosgenin. This plant steroid is widely used in the pharmaceutical industry to synthesize steroidal hormones, including those used in birth control pills
Open area 2L.funFact: Not Sweet Potatoes! In the United States, orange-fleshed sweet potatoes are frequently mislabeled and sold as "yams". True yams are starchy with a bark-like, rough skin, whereas sweet potatoes are much sweeter and have a thin, smooth skin.

Open area 2M.uses: Insect Repellent: The oil contains natural compounds (like citronellal, geraniol, and limonene) that mask human odors, effectively deterring mosquitoes and other biting bugs [1].Aromatherapy: Used in diffusers to create a calming, refreshing atmosphere and to help relieve mental fatigue.Skincare & Cosmetics: Diluted into soaps, lotions, and massage oils [2]. It has natural antifungal and antibacterial properties that help cleanse the skin.
Open area 2M.funFact: Not a single plant: People often assume citronella is a specific plant, but it is actually a tall, clumping grass similar to lemongrass

Open area 2N.uses: Culinary: The mushroom-flavored flowers are a popular, quirky addition to fresh salads. The tough flower spikes can also be used as a seasoning in soups and stews much like a bay leaf.Traditional Medicine: Historically used by indigenous and folk healers as a "cooling tonic". Leaves are frequently steeped into teas or decoctions to help soothe gastrointestinal discomfort, clear respiratory issues, and promote relaxation
Open area 2N.funFact: It tastes like mushrooms: The tiny, delicate flowers can be eaten raw and have a surprisingly distinct, earthy, mushroom-like flavor.It has a beer connection: The common name "porterweed" comes from the dark, foamy, beer-like infusion that can be made from brewing its leaves.

Open area 2O.uses: Culinary & Beverages: The soft, white flesh is blended into refreshing smoothies, juices, ice creams, and jams. It has a unique flavor often described as a mix of strawberry, pineapple, and citrus.Traditional Medicine: In many tropical regions, teas made from the leaves and bark are used to treat ailments like inflammation, fevers, and insomnia.v
Open area 2O.funFact: Electric Leaves: The leaves and roots of the soursop tree are known to contain chemical compounds (annonacins) that are highly toxic to certain pests. Studies have shown they can even disrupt the nervous systems of small insects.

Open area 2P.uses: This plant is a powerhouse in traditional medicine and regional cuisines across South and Southeast Asia:Medicinal Tea: The leaves are frequently brewed into a health-promoting tea, particularly in Thailand, to manage conditions like diabetes and rheumatism.
Open area 2P.funFact: VapoRub Scent: When its leaves are crushed, they release a powerful, medicinal odor similar to camphor or Vicks VapoRub, which gives the plant its name.Antioxidant Powerhouse: Research suggests that tea made from Pluchea indica leaves can have stronger antioxidant properties than even green tea (Camellia sinensis). Coastal Guardian: This plant thrives in harsh, salty environments like mangroves and salt marshes, playing a vital role in maintaining the ecological balance of coastal areas.Natural Insect Repellent: Because of its pungent chemical glands, the plant is naturally resistant to deer and is often used as a biological insect repellent.

openarea2Q.uses: Traditionally, various parts of the plant are used in Ayurvedic and other traditional systems of medicine to treat skin complaints, diarrhea, vertigo, fever, and body aches.  The ripe, dark purple or black berries are edible and have a tart, pleasant taste. They are sometimes used in jams and jellies.
openarea2Q.funFact: The fruit is a favorite snack of the bandicoot, a small marsupial, which gives the plant its common name, Bandicoot Berry.

Open area 2R.uses: When ripe, they are dark red or purple, crunchy, and refreshing, similar to an apple. Used in soups, stews, porridges, and as a filling for Chinese desserts like mooncakes and mochi.
Open area 2R.funFact: Jujube fruit , also known as red dates  is a highly nutritious, versatile fruit cultivated for over 4,000 years, primarily in Asia

Open area 2S.uses: Digestive Aid: Chewing fresh leaves after meals stimulates saliva and digestive juices. It helps reduce bloating and constipation.Oral Hygiene: Naturally antibacterial, the leaf helps combat oral pathogens that cause cavities, gum disease, and bad breath.Respiratory Relief: It has anti-inflammatory and expectorant properties. Applying a warm poultice to the chest or consuming the leaf juice with honey can help relieve coughs and chest congestion.Wound Healing: Applied topically as a crushed paste, it acts as an antiseptic to promote faster healing of small cuts and skin infections.
Open area 2S.funFact: Green Gold": Because of its widespread daily consumption and numerous health benefits, it is sometimes referred to as the "Green Gold" of India.The Fourth Most Popular Drug: Betel chewing (wrapping the leaf with the areca/betel nut and slaked lime) is considered the fourth most popular psychoactive drug in the world, surpassed only by nicotine, alcohol, and caffeine.

Open area 2U.uses: Traditional Medicine: The plant has a long history in Southeast Asian and Javanese traditional medicine. Leaves, twigs, and sap are often used in poultices to soothe fevers, heal wounds, treat headaches, and address bodily pain.
Open area 2U.funFact: Thorny All the Way: Unlike many other Leea species, L. angulata is fiercely protected by sharp, triangular prickles that cover not just its trunk and main branches, but its ultimate, tender branches as well.Grape Family Ties: It belongs to the Vitaceae family (the grape family). However, unlike its trailing or climbing grapevine cousins, it grows as a strong, upright, multi-stemmed shrub or tree.Critically Endangered in Singapore: If you are based in Punggol or elsewhere in Singapore, it might be very hard to spot. In local botany records, the plant is listed as Critically Endangered in the wild, with only a few pockets of adult individuals documented (such as around the Lower Seletar Reservoir).

Open area 2V.uses: The flowers are a specialty ingredient in Thai, Vietnamese, and Filipino cuisine. They are commonly cooked into omelets, stir-fried with oyster sauce, or used in soups.
Open area 2V.funFact: The flowers emit a very strong, pleasant citrus-like fragrance, particularly during the evening. This oil is extracted to create perfumes and in floral, aromatic gardens. That is why its Chinese name is 夜来香

Open area 2W.uses: Culinary & Snacks: Eaten roasted or salted, and blended into pastes as the creamy base for Indian curries (like Korma)
Open area 2W.funFact: They Are Not True Nuts: Botanically, the cashew is actually a drupe (a seed that grows on the outside of a false fruit), rather than a traditional nut.A Poison Ivy Relative: The cashew tree is in the Anacardiaceae family, meaning it shares a botanical lineage with pistachios, mangoes, and toxic plants like poison ivy and poison oak

Open area 2X.uses: Fresh Eating: The fruit is typically eaten fresh; it is scooped out and best served chilled.
Open area 2X.funFact: The "Star" Pattern: When the fruit is sliced in half horizontally, the core and seeds create a beautiful, distinct star-like pattern.

Open area 2Y.uses: Fresh Eating: Sliced raw and eaten fresh, often used as a garnish in salads, fruit platters, and cocktails.
Open area 2Y.funFact: Dietary Precaution: People with kidney problems or chronic kidney disease should avoid star fruit National Kidney Foundation. The fruit contains a neurotoxin (carambotoxin) and high levels of oxalates that healthy kidneys easily filter out, but can be dangerous or cause severe hiccups, vomiting, and confusion in individuals with kidney dysfunction.

Open area 2Z.uses: Culinary: Used to flavor baked goods, salads, and marinades, and to preserve jams. The fresh juice is also a staple for making lemonade and flavoring teas
Open area 2Z.funFact: Glowing Spark: When the oils from a lemon peel are squeezed near an open flame, the compounds (specifically limonene) ignite to create a tiny spark, essentially functioning as a natural firework.

Open area 2ZB.uses: Culinary Snack (Emping): The mature seeds are ground into flour and deep-fried to create emping, a popular, slightly bitter Indonesian cracker.
Open area 2ZB.funFact: An Imposter "Fruit": Melinjo does not produce true fruits or flowers. It is a gymnosperm (related to pine trees), meaning its "fruits" are actually colorful, fleshy seed cones.

Open area 2ZC.uses: Culinary: Highly sour, it is used as a natural souring agent (like tamarind) in Asian curries, fish stews, and sambals. In Southeast Asia and the Philippines, the raw fruit is often dipped in rock salt or made into sweet jams and pickles.Traditional Medicine: The leaves, fruit, and flowers are used in folk medicine to treat coughs, high blood pressure, and skin conditions (like itchy rashes or mumps).
Open area 2ZC.funFact: Grows from the trunk: Unlike most fruits that hang from branches, belimbing fruits grow in heavy, clustered groups directly on the tree trunk and main branches.High productivity: A single tree can produce an astonishing 45 to 50 kg of fruit in a year.

Open area 2ZD.uses: Beverage production: Roasted and ground seeds are brewed into global beverage variants.Caffeine extraction: Isolates are utilized in pharmaceuticals, energy drinks, and supplements.
Open area 2ZD.funFact: Fruit origins: Coffee beans are actually seeds found inside bright red fruits called "coffee cherries".Goat discovery: Legend says 9th-century Ethiopian herders discovered coffee after seeing goats "dance" from eating the berries.

Open area 3D.uses: Fresh Eating: The fruit is typically eaten fresh; it is scooped out and best served chilled.
Open area 3D.funFact: The "Star" Pattern: When the fruit is sliced in half horizontally, the core and seeds create a beautiful, distinct star-like pattern.

Open area 1B.uses: Ornamental: A highly popular outdoor hedge or patio container plant in tropical and subtropical regions, and a coveted novelty houseplant in colder climates.
Open area 1B.funFact: Thomas Edison historically experimented with this plant alongside hundreds of others while trying to source a domestic alternative for natural rubber.

Open area 1C.uses: Wound Healing: Often called the "soldier's herb," the leaves are applied topically to minor wounds, insect bites, and ulcers to stop bleeding and ward off infections
Open area 1C.funFact: According to legend, the plant gets its name from a wounded 19th-century Spanish soldier named Matico. After learning from local Indigenous tribes in Peru that applying the plant's leaves to his battle wounds stopped the bleeding, the herb quickly gained the nickname soldier's herb

Open area 1D.uses: Culinary: The fruit rind and soft flesh are edible. Sweet varieties are eaten fresh (sometimes dipped in chili salt), while sour varieties are stewed, candied, or used as souring agents in dishes like Filipino sinigang or ginataang santol and Thai curries.
Open area 1D.funFact: The Toxic Seed Hazard: While the fluffy white pulp is delicious, the large seeds are toxic and must not be swallowed. Swallowing them whole has caused severe intestinal obstruction, occasionally requiring abdominal surgery.

Open area 1F.uses: Fresh Consumption: Eaten raw as a thirst-quenching snack, often sprinkled with salt or chili, or sliced into tropical fruit salads
Open area 1F.funFact: Super Hydrating: The fruit consists of up to 91% water, making it an excellent natural hydrator during hot weather

Open area 1G.uses: Natural Dye: The leaves and stems contain a compound called indican, which has been used for centuries to produce the famous natural blue dye known as "Assam Indigo".Traditional Medicine: The rhizomes, roots, and leaves are staples in traditional Chinese medicine (known as Nan Ban Lan Gen or Qingdai). They are used to make herbal decoctions and poultices for their anti-inflammatory, detoxifying, and antiviral properties.
Open area 1G.funFact: Historically, indigenous cultures combined the blue dye extracted from its twigs with turmeric to create green dyes, or with safflower to create rich purple hues.
